newsitem.title: CONGO: AFRICAN REFUGEES FLEE FEAR OF KINSHASA MELTDOWN.
newsitem.headline: AFRICAN REFUGEES FLEE FEAR OF KINSHASA MELTDOWN.

text.p: Thousands of African expatriates fearing looting and murder have fled Zaire's capital for neighbouring Congo as rebels advance towards the city.
Police sources said that 4,000 Malians arrived at Brazzaville's Maya Maya airport on Friday night, trying to get back to their impoverished West African homeland.
Exhausted women and tiny children lay down and slept where they could among suitcases and bundles of belongings as they waited to find out where they would be going next.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who failed to show up for talks with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko on a ship off Congo on Friday, said Kinshasa could fall to his troops within two weeks.
Kabila on Wednesday told Reuters the advance would only be halted if Mobutu stepped down.
Rebels say they have airlifted extra troops and weapons into Kikwit, only 400 km (250 miles) from Kinshasa and are moving closer to the teeming capital of five million people.

Residents say Mobutu's ragged and demoralised army has already left Kenge, just 200 km (125 miles) east of the capital -- true to the form which has driven it from more than three quarters of the vast state since October.
As much as a last stand by the army, Zaireans and expatriates alike fear the troops will live up to their reputation for stealing what they can before fleeing.
Two rounds of army-led looting in 1991 and 1993 killed hundreds of people while business virtually collapsed -- never to regain its previous level.
Immigrants from impoverished West African countries, mainly Mali, Senegal and Guinea, first moved to Zaire in the 1970s when the mineral-rich state was awash with money from copper and cobalt mines.
Coming from countries much poorer than Zaire they set up businesses selling everything from grilled meat to the latest fashion clothes to magic potions.

Even as years of corruption, ethnic and political violence put paid to Zaire's prosperity, the West Africans thrived from close connections with the powerful and through their place in the lifeline diamond trade.
